newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper clashes with court over economy.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper clashes with court over economy.

text.p: President Ernesto Samper clashed with Colombia's highest court on Thursday, accusing it of political meddling after it overturned his three-month-old emergency economic plan on grounds it was unconstitutional.

Government finances were left in disarray by the Constitutional Court ruling Wednesday night and Samper, who has been dogged allegations that he used drug money to finance his presidential campaign, said he had no doubt that it was politically motivated.
"For me it was a political decision," Samper told reporters. "It's a decision that questions the government's ability to manage the economy."

Samper's ruling Liberal Party dominates Congress and he vowed, in reprisal for the move, to propose a constitutional amendment stripping the court of all power to determine when a president is legitimately empowered to rule by decree.

The court responded, in a statement issued shortly after Samper's public outburst, that it was "deeply surprised by the president's statements" since its ruling was "framed within strict constitutional mandates" and was neither "improvised nor the fruit of prejudice."
It added that it viewed with "deep concern" Samper's bid to set himself up as "a judge of decisions taken by those who are responsible for upholding the supremacy and integrity of the constitution."

The clash between the executive and judicial branch came after the court, in a 6-3 vote Wednesday night, struck down all 16 decrees issued under the state of economic emergency Samper declared on Jan. 13 to help fight a yawning fiscal deficit running at 4 percent of gross domestic product.

The court ruled that all of problems relating to the fiscal deficit were foreseeable and not the result of unforeseen circumstances warranting emergency rule. In order to apply, the emergency measures must be approved by Congress on a case-by-case basis, it said.

Business leaders had almost unanimously criticised the package of emergency measures, which included a 6 percent tax on all new foreign loans, as something that would drive up import costs, put inflationary pressure on the economy and hamper Colombia's economic opening.
They also bridled against the uncertainty it created since the government had rammed through measures without the prior approval of Congress.
"The court has called attention in this way to the possibility of opening the door to a fiscal dictatorship," said Sabas Pretelt de la Vega, president of the National Federation of Businessmen.

Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo said the government would move quickly to win congressional approval of all the measures it annnounced in January. But in the meantime, he faces the likelihood of having to give back millions of dollars collected since January through the new tax on foreign credits and a 16 percent sales tax on previously exempt services provided in Colombia by foreign-based companies.

The tax on foreign loans was aimed, in part, at avoiding a new surge in the peso, which strengthened substantially to the deteriment of exporters late last year on huge inflows of foreign capital. To avoid another run up, now that the tax has been eliminated, the central bank hastily ruled Wednesday night that 50 percent of any new foreign loans with a duration of less than five years must be deposited with it for 18 months.

To help shore up its finances, the government also announced late Thursday that it was temporarily raising Colombia's import tariffs. The measure, called "a very serious mistake" by Pretelt de la Vega, will remain in effect for at least 90 days.
